subtype: Approach: comply quietly to avoid conflict [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Darshan,

I need to write this down because I can't say it out loud. Last Thursday my manager asked me to backdate the vendor form before the audit. I was scared for my job, my rent is due and there is nobody at home who could cover it. So I did it and told no one.

I thought I would feel relief. I feel a small stone in my stomach. Every time the auditors' email comes up, my hands go cold. Today my manager hinted at another form. I now understand that quiet compliance isn't free: I am the one whose name is on it, and I'm the one who'll be asked.

Don't tell anyone yet. I just needed someone to know.

Uma

qa.q: What did Uma's manager ask for last Thursday?
qa.a: To backdate the vendor form before the audit.

qa.q: How is Uma feeling since backdating the form?
qa.a: Uma feels anxious and guilty, described as a small stone in the stomach and cold hands whenever the auditors' email appears.

qa.q: What could Uma do now instead of waiting for the next request, and why?
qa.a: Uma could talk with someone trusted, such as a senior or an ethics contact, about correcting the record, because the risk grows if the pattern continues.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel on getting this letter?
qa.a: Darshan may feel worried and honoured to be trusted, though also uneasy about keeping the secret when Uma may need help.

grounding: Afraid of losing the job, the employee backdates the form and tells no one, then carries the worry of an audit and a repeat request.

subtype: Approach: comply quietly to avoid conflict [Pitfall]
passage:
Vinita, I have to tell someone, so it's you. I'm Payal, and three weeks ago I did something I'm not proud of.
My manager asked me to put an earlier date on a supplier contract, so it looked signed before the audit period. I said, 'Okay, sir.' That's it. Two words. I was so scared of being the new girl who makes trouble, of losing the job I waited a year for. So I changed it, printed it, filed it. I told no one.
Since then I can't sleep properly. Every time the audit team walks past, my stomach drops. It's my initials on the file, not his.
And yesterday he came to my desk again. Another contract. 'Same as last time, na?' As if it's normal now. As if I'm the person who does that.
I said I'd do it after lunch. I didn't. It's still on my desk.
So that's why I called you, Vinita. I don't know how to undo it. I only know I can't do it again.

qa.q: What did Payal's manager ask her to do?
qa.a: Put an earlier date on a supplier contract.
Guilty and frightened, losing sleep and dreading the audit team, especially since her initials are on the file.

qa.q: What could Payal do now about both contracts?
qa.a: Leave the second one unchanged, write down both requests, and talk to a trusted senior, HR or the ethics channel about correcting the first.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel hearing this?
qa.a: Worried for Payal but glad she spoke up, and likely keen to help her find the right person to tell.

grounding: Shows an employee who quietly backdated a document out of fear for the job, now carrying guilt and audit risk and being asked again.

I'm Pema, and I sit across from Farida in the accounts team. I saw the day it started, though I didn't understand it then.
In June our team lead leaned over her desk and said something quietly. Farida's face went still. She nodded, pulled up a payment voucher, changed something and printed it. She didn't look at anyone for the rest of the afternoon.
After that she changed. She stopped joining us for lunch. She jumped when the internal audit team came to our floor in July, and spent most of their visit in the washroom. Twice I saw her open that same folder and close it again without doing anything.
In August the team lead leaned over her desk again. This time she said, 'Can I think about it?' and he walked off looking annoyed.
Later, by the lift, she asked me, 'Have you ever done something at work you wish you could take back?' I said we could talk after work if she wanted. She said maybe.

qa.q: When did the internal audit team come to the floor?
What might Farida's staying in the washroom during the audit suggest?
qa.a: She seems frightened and guilty, afraid the changed voucher might be found.

qa.q: What could Farida do now, instead of carrying it alone?
qa.a: Talk to someone she trusts, like Pema, and then to HR or the ethics channel about the earlier voucher before being asked again.

qa.q: How does the whole thing look to Pema?
qa.a: Pema notices the changes in Farida without knowing the cause, and gently offers to talk, unsure whether she will.

grounding: Shows an employee who quietly changed a record to avoid conflict, then lives with fear of the audit and is asked again.
